page.title: Invoked services
page.description: Run a connection, a subprocess or a long computation for as long as a chart's state is active, with SCXML's invoke.

hero.headline: Run a service while a state is active.
hero.lede: A chart's <invoke> starts a service your program runs when the state is entered and stops it when the state is left. 200,000 actors with a service each made a million round trips in 18 to 23 seconds.

section.heading: Use invoke for what outlives one send.
section.p: An I/O processor answers one send at a time. A connection, a subprocess, a long computation or a subscription lives longer.
SCXML's <invoke> starts it on entering a state and stops it on leaving. While the state is active, the chart and the service exchange events.
When the invoked thing is another chart, the host runs it as a child actor (A chart that starts another). When your program runs it, it is a service, and this guide is about those.

section.heading: Return a service from the type's handler.
section.p: The host's options register a handler per <invoke type>: services: { [type]: handler }. At each start the handler gets an invocation and returns the service, any object.
The host keeps the service until the invocation ends and calls its two methods, both optional:

item.text: gets each <send target="#_<invokeid>"> of the invoker, and each event it forwards with autoforward="true";
runs when the invoker leaves the state, which cancels the invocation.

section.p: The service talks back through the invocation. invocation.sendBack(event, data) sends the invoker an event whose _event.invokeid is the invoke's id.
invocation.done(data) ends the service and gives the invoker done.invoke.<invokeid> with data:

example.code: started urn:example:counter counter://local for session 1 pong 11 from counter pong 12 from counter done, total 13

section.p: A service that ended with done is not stopped: stop runs only for a cancel.

section.heading: Send to a service from a later event.
section.p: An invocation starts at the end of the macrostep that entered its state, as a child chart does. Anything that macrostep sends to it comes before the service exists.
So a <send target="#_counter"> in the state's own <onentry>, a raised event's transition or an eventless one gets error.communication. Send from a later event, as go does above.

section.heading: Keep the invocation while the service runs.
section.p: The invocation is a record, so a service may keep it and call sendBack from a timer or a promise. It holds these fields:

item.text: the <param>s as an object, or the <content>;
true when a restored host starts it again ().

section.p: sendBack and done continue the invoke's trace unless their last argument is { traceparent }. A null traceparent starts a new trace.
After done, a cancel or host.close(), both throw a TinyactorsError with TA_ERROR_STALE.
The send receive gets is a view, as an I/O processor's is: read it during the call. A receive that returns a promise has its send filled first, so it may read it after an await.

section.heading: Return a promise while the service connects.
section.p: A handler may return a promise of the service, while a connection opens or a process spawns. Until it settles the sends wait, and reach receive in order once it resolves.
The invocation may sendBack meanwhile, as this handler does with status:

example.code: status connecting db://primary says yes to first db://primary says yes to second

item.term: A cancel before the promise settles
item.text: stops the service as soon as it resolves. The sends that waited are dropped, since the invoker has left and nothing could answer them.
is a failed start: the invoker gets error.communication, once and once more for each send that waited. The rejection stays unhandled, as any handler's promise's does (Before you use it).
a promise that settles is ignored.

section.heading: Or return it at once and await inside.
section.p: A service returned at once takes sends before it is ready, and decides itself what a send does while it connects. Its methods await its own start:
await host.idle() waits for the promises your handlers return, a service handler's or a receive's. It does not wait for one a service starts on its own.
Both examples open the connection in the background, so they wait on a timer first.

section.heading: Every failure reaches the invoker.
section.p: Each of these gives the invoker error.communication, and so does each later send until the invoker leaves the state:

item.text: no handler for the type, or none for a restored invocation;
a handler that throws or whose promise rejects;
a receive that throws or whose promise rejects: the service crashed, and is dropped without stop.

section.p: The invoker gets none when it cancelled the invocation in the same step that started it.
A handler's error is reported after the turn, to onHandlerError(error, invocation) or out of idle(). A type with no handler throws nothing.
The chart chose the type, and naming one you do not serve must not let a chart end your process. An untrusted chart on quickjs could do that otherwise.

example.code: idle() rejected: no SMTP server the mail service failed

section.p: host.close() drops the running services without calling stop. The host keeps them on its own object, so a dropped host whose services refer back to it is still collected.
An invocation uses one of the host's requests. system.maxRequests is where the pool starts, and a segment grows it when it runs out ().

section.heading: A round trip costs the same at 200,000.
section.p: tools/services.mjs runs actors that each invoke a counter service, and sends pings and pongs to actors drawn at random. Then a third finish with done data, a third are cancelled, and the rest keep theirs.
It checks that every pong is counted once and every done datum is right. Every cancelled service must be stopped exactly once, no other stopped, and the ended services collected.

table.caption: 200,000 actors, each with a counter service, making 1,000,000 round trips (actor, service, actor); then a third finished and a third cancelled. Every check passed, and the host held only the 66,666 services still running. One run, alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5, Bun 1.4.1.

section.p: A round trip costs about what it costs with 10,000 actors. A run's work does not grow with the running invocations.
In the repository, mise run services runs the program.
